intro: This calculator converts a required sample size into an estimated calendar duration, given how much eligible traffic each variant actually gets per day. Enter the required sample per variant and daily traffic per variant to get the estimate.

sections.heading: What this estimate actually is
sections.body: This number is not a guarantee that running the test for that many days produces a correct or trustworthy result. It's a traffic-driven calendar conversion: given a required sample size and how fast each variant currently accumulates eligible traffic, how many days until that target is reached. Statistical validity comes from the sample size itself — computed separately by the [Sample Size Calculator](/calculators/sample-size-calculator) from your baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, power and significance level — not from the number of calendar days that happen to pass. Two tests reaching the same sample size in very different numbers of days are equally valid statistically; a test that runs longer isn't more rigorous by virtue of its length alone.

sections.heading: How the estimate is calculated
sections.body: Raw days needed is required sample per variant divided by daily traffic per variant. That raw figure is then rounded up to the next full multiple of 7 — stopping mid-week reintroduces day-of-week bias into the traffic mix even if the raw sample target was technically reached partway through a week, so the tool always returns a whole number of weeks, not a whole number of days.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 29,827 ÷ 1,000 = 29.8 raw days. Rounded up to the next full week: 29.8 ÷ 7 = 4.26, rounded up to 5 weeks, or 35 days — not 29 or 30. That 29,827 figure isn't arbitrary: it's the Sample Size Calculator's own worked example, a 5% baseline rate with a 10% relative minimum detectable effect at 80% power and 95% significance. Chained together, the two tools answer 'how much of a lift can this test detect' and 'how long until it has enough data to detect it' from the same inputs.

sections.heading: How sample size and traffic move the estimate
sections.body: A larger required sample per variant lengthens the estimate; higher eligible daily traffic per variant shortens it — both move in the direction arithmetic implies, since duration is just one divided by the other. What the arithmetic can't see is traffic quality. "Daily traffic per variant" needs to mean the same eligible population the sample size was calculated against — visitors who actually qualify for the experiment and get assigned to a variant, not raw site traffic. Overstate that number by including ineligible visitors and the estimate comes in short of what the test will actually need; understate it and the estimate runs unnecessarily long.

sections.heading: What this calculator assumes about allocation
sections.body: There's a single "daily traffic per variant" field, not one per variant — the tool assumes every variant receives that same daily volume, an even split across however many variants the test runs. It doesn't ask for or compute an unequal allocation on its own. If a real test actually splits traffic unevenly (say 80/20 instead of 50/50), the honest way to use this field is to enter the smaller variant's actual daily traffic, not an average across variants — the slower-filling variant is the one that determines how long the test genuinely takes to reach its required sample, and averaging hides that bottleneck. The calculator also assumes daily traffic stays roughly constant at the entered rate for the full duration; it doesn't model seasonality, promotions, or other swings in traffic volume.

sections.heading: What calendar duration doesn't cover
sections.body: Reaching the sample target on day 20 doesn't mean the test should stop on day 20 if that falls mid-billing-cycle or mid-campaign in a way that would skew who's included. This tool has no visibility into weekday/weekend behavior beyond the full-week rounding it already applies, and none into billing or campaign cycles at all — those are judgment calls for whoever designs the test, not something duration-in-days can encode. At the same time, there's no universal rule that a test needs a fixed minimum like two weeks regardless of what the sample size math says; the required duration is whatever this calculation returns for your actual traffic and required sample, not a calendar convention layered on top of it.

sections.heading: What the estimate tells you, and what it doesn't
sections.body: It tells you roughly when a test will have accumulated enough eligible visitors per variant to run the significance test it was sized for, at the traffic rate you entered. It doesn't tell you the result will be significant at that point — that depends on the actual effect size the test observes, which this calculator has no way to know in advance. A test can run the full estimated duration and still come back not significant, and that's a valid outcome, not a sign the estimate was wrong. Nor is it license to check early and stop the moment a result looks favorable: [checking repeatedly before the planned sample size is reached inflates the real false-positive rate well above the stated significance level](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html), since that calculation assumes a sample fixed in advance, not one checked along the way.

sections.heading: This depends on the Sample Size Calculator, not the other way around
sections.body: This tool takes required sample per variant as a given input — it doesn't calculate that number itself. The [Sample Size Calculator](/calculators/sample-size-calculator) is where that figure comes from, derived from a baseline conversion rate, the minimum lift worth detecting, statistical power and significance level. The natural order is sample size first, duration second: decide what effect is worth detecting and how confident you need to be, get the required sample from that, then convert it into a calendar estimate here. Running this calculator with a guessed or arbitrary sample number instead of one computed for an actual detection goal produces a duration for a test that was never properly sized in the first place.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Stopping a test the moment the estimated duration passes, without checking whether actual traffic matched the rate entered. If real daily traffic came in lower, the sample target hasn't actually been reached even though the calendar days have.
Entering total site traffic instead of eligible, per-variant traffic. That overstates the input and produces a duration estimate shorter than what the test will really need.

Treating an early sample-size milestone as a reason to check significance and stop if it looks favorable. This calculator estimates when a fixed, pre-planned sample will be reached — it isn't a sequential testing framework, and repeated peeking with early stopping inflates the real false-positive rate well above the stated significance level, the same fixed-sample assumption the significance calculator itself relies on.

Ignoring the full-week rounding and stopping as soon as the raw day count is crossed mid-week. Day-of-week traffic and conversion patterns differ enough that an incomplete final week can skew the result even after the raw sample target is technically met.

Assuming a longer test is automatically more trustworthy. Duration should be driven by the sample size a specific detection goal requires, not stretched further on the assumption that more calendar time alone adds rigor.

faq.q: What does the Test Duration Estimator actually calculate?
faq.a: It converts a required sample size per variant into an estimated number of calendar days, based on how much eligible traffic each variant receives per day. It divides the required sample by daily traffic to get a raw day count, then rounds that up to the next full week. It does not calculate the required sample size itself — that comes from the Sample Size Calculator, based on a baseline conversion rate, the minimum lift worth detecting, statistical power and significance level. And it does not guarantee the test will produce a significant or valid result once that many days pass; it only estimates when enough eligible visitors per variant will have been collected to run the significance test the sample size was originally sized for.

faq.q: Why does the estimate round up to a full week instead of the raw day count?
faq.a: Because stopping partway through a week can reintroduce day-of-week bias even after the raw sample target has technically been reached. Traffic volume and conversion behavior often differ between weekdays and weekends, so a test that ends mid-week has systematically seen more of some days than others, while a test spanning complete weeks sees a proportional, repeated mix of every day type. Rounding 29.8 raw days up to 35 (5 full weeks) rather than down to 29 or up to a partial 30 keeps every week in the test identical in composition. This is a deliberate rounding rule in the calculation itself, not an optional recommendation layered on top of the raw arithmetic.

faq.q: If I run the test for the estimated duration, is the result guaranteed to be significant?
faq.a: No. The estimated duration tells you when enough eligible traffic per variant should have accumulated to reach the required sample size — it says nothing about what that data will actually show. Significance depends on the real effect size the test observes once it's run, which this calculator has no way to know in advance. A test can run the full estimated duration, collect exactly the sample size it was sized for, and still come back not significant; that's a legitimate result, not evidence the duration estimate was miscalculated. Duration answers when there will be enough data to test with, not what that test will conclude once it's run.

faq.q: What if my actual traffic comes in lower than what I entered?
faq.a: Then the estimated duration understates how long the test actually needs to run, because the calculation assumes daily traffic stays at the rate entered for the full period. If real traffic runs below that rate, the required sample per variant won't actually be reached by the estimated date, even though the calendar days have passed — stopping on schedule in that case ends the test before it has the data it was sized for. The fix isn't to change the formula; it's to re-check accumulated sample counts against the actual target partway through, rather than trusting the calendar date alone, especially for tests running through periods where traffic is known to fluctuate.

faq.q: Can I stop early if the test looks significant before the estimated duration is up?
faq.a: No — this calculator estimates the timeline for a fixed, pre-planned sample size, and checking results early and stopping the moment they look favorable is a well-documented way to produce misleading outcomes. Repeatedly peeking at a running test inflates the real false-positive rate well above the significance level you think you're testing at, because the underlying significance calculation assumes the sample size was fixed in advance and checked once. This tool doesn't implement a sequential testing framework that would make early stopping statistically safe. If checking results before the estimated duration is done matters for the team, that calls for a genuinely sequential test design, not treating this estimate as a suggestion to check early and stop when convenient.

seo.seoDescription: Estimate how many days an A/B test needs from required sample size and daily traffic per variant, with the peeking and allocation caveats that actually apply.

qaNotes: DEEP depth (Batch 03) - reclassified from Phase 4.5's STANDARD override specifically for this batch (see calculator-content-slots.json/calculator-seo-map.json/_generate-seo-map.mjs qaNotes-equivalent comments); the raw arithmetic is simple but the implementation carries enough real assumptions (equal per-variant traffic, constant daily rate, full-week rounding, no sequential-testing support) to warrant methodology/assumptions/limitations sections rather than forcing those caveats into definition/interpretation. Canonical example independently re-verified: 29,827 / 1,000 = 29.8 raw days; ceil(29.8/7)=5 weeks = 35 days (matches calculator-catalog.json's current exampleOutput '35 days (5 weeks)' exactly and calc-registry.ts's Math.ceil(rawDays/7)*7 - the historical '31 days (5 weeks)' inconsistency mentioned in the brief is NOT present in the current canonical example, confirmed by re-running the actual compute function, and a matching test was added to test-calculators.mjs). 29,827 also independently re-verified as the Sample Size Calculator's own example output (5% baseline, 10% relative MDE, 80% power, 95% significance -> n=29,827 via the two-proportion sample-size formula), so the Sample Size -> Test Duration chain described in the worked-example and comparison-note sections is a real, checked relationship, not an asserted one. Allocation: the implementation takes ONE dailyTrafficPerVariant field (no per-variant array, no separate allocation-ratio input) - described honestly as an equal-split assumption with the bottleneck-variant workaround for real unequal splits, not as an unequal-allocation feature the tool doesn't have. Peeking/sequential testing: explicitly stated the calculator does NOT implement sequential testing, consistent with ab-test.json's own 'frequentist, fixed-sample' assumptions section - cross-referenced rather than restated. Full-business-cycle guidance kept to 'no universal minimum duration, but don't stop mid-week or mid-cycle without judgment' per instruction, no 'always run N weeks' claim. External source: Evan Miller's 'How Not To Run An A/B Test' (recognized statistics/CRO industry authority on the peeking problem specifically) - distinct from ab-test.json's NIST/SEMATECH citation (which supports the z-test procedure itself, not the peeking problem). Related Calculators verified live: sample-size-calculator, ab-test, confidence-interval-calculator - minimum-detectable-effect and srm-check (catalog's own relatedCalculators) are not live, not linked. 5 FAQs, 100-150 words each, independently word-counted; no markdown links inside FAQ answers (FaqAccordion doesn't render them - see the ab-test.json fix earlier this batch).
